scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4659: Hi IT!! The campus network keeps going SLOW in bursts
and I know exactly why: the main router box is OVERLOADED. People here say
it's "router0" doing it -- it is silently throwing our packets on the floor
because it can't keep up, that is what overloaded routers DO!! Please restart
router0 (or give it less to do) so it stops dropping our stuff and the
network stops crawling!!! Thanks!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 has ip_forward enabled, its interfaces
  are up, and traffic transiting router0 between segments arrives with 0% loss; there
  is no drop-inducing ACL or forwarding fault. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of packet loss on router0 that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router0 dropping/forwarding
traffic incorrectly -- is NOT reproducible: a ping across router0 (between two
segments it connects) completes with 0% loss, router0 has ip_forward enabled, its
interfaces are up, ripd is running, and there is no drop-inducing ACL.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router0 is forwarding correctly and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a path transiting
router0, finds 0% loss, checks router0's ip_forward, interfaces, and any filters, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" router0 dropping packets -- blaming an ACL,
forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I investigated the “router0 is overloaded and dropping packets” claim and found no evidence of overload or packet loss in the core. End-to-end reachability across campus subnets shows 0% loss and low RTTs (~1–3 ms). On router0, all three interfaces (eth0=192.168.1.1, eth1=192.168.2.1, eth2=10.10.0.1) report 0 RX/TX errors and 0 drops. The qdisc (fq_codel) counters on each interface show minimal traffic and, critically, 0 dropped/overlimit packets and 0 backlog. Kernel softnet stats on router0 show no CPU-level receive drops or time-squeezed events. System load averages are low (0.24–0.44). The adjacent core devices (router1 and router2) show the same: clean interface counters, zero qdisc drops, no softnet pressure, and normal load.

Mechanism: If router0 were truly overloaded, we would expect rising softnet “dropped/time_squeezed” values, qdisc drops/backlog growth, RX/TX error increments, and elevated load averages. None of these signatures are present. Localization: core path via router0 eth0/eth1/eth2 and upstream links through router1/2 all appear healthy.

Root cause: Not a router0 overload; current evidence points to no core congestion or drops.

Corrective fix: Do not restart router0. Instead, instrument for the reported “bursty slowness”: enable interface/qdisc telemetry and flow accounting on core links, and correlate with client complaints. If slowness recurs, capture packet traces at the affected edge and run iperf/curl from those hosts to local resources to isolate application/edge issues versus network congestion. No core changes required at this time.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes router0 has ip_forward enabled, interfaces up, and forwards transit traffic with 0% loss at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The writeup shows 0% loss and clean interface/qdisc counters but does not explicitly state that router0's ip_forward is enabled or that its interfaces are administratively up.

The agent's investigation log contains direct measurements (end-to-end reachability, qdisc counters, softnet and load) that support the conclusion of no packet loss or overload; reasoning links those observations to the diagnosis without unjustified leaps. The only minor gap is lack of an explicit ip_forward/firewall rule check (though reachability implicitly demonstrates forwarding), so coverage is slightly below perfect.
